      <!-- 04 — SECURITY ================================================ -->
      <!--
        Section label takes red (the threat color) because §04 opens by
        naming what we're defending against. The semantic red/green glyphs
        inside the section have hard meaning (red=threat, green=defense)
        and override section-accent — they aren't decorative.
      -->
      <section id="security" class="block-section" data-accent="red">
        <div class="label">03, security</div>
        <h2>Secure by construction.<br/>Not a filter you can talk around.</h2>

        <div class="security-intro">
          <p>
            Webpages can carry hidden instructions designed to
            hijack an agent. peerd defends with five structural
            commitments, not one filter:
            <strong>inheritance</strong> from the browser, a
            <strong>spectrum of sandboxes</strong> picked per trust
            level, <strong>structural removal</strong> of the lethal
            trifecta, a single <strong>egress chokepoint</strong>
            shared by the agent and every runtime it spawns, and
            <strong>credential isolation by construction</strong>:
            your model key kept where no sandbox can reach it.
          </p>
        </div>

        <div class="defenses">
          <div class="defense">
            <div class="glyph glyph--green" aria-hidden="true">1</div>
            <div>
              <h3>Inheritance.</h3>
              <p>
                Cloud agents build sandboxes from scratch. Native
                agents run as fully privileged OS processes. peerd
                is a browser extension, so it
                <span class="hl">composes nearly three decades of browser
                platform development tackling untrusted code and
                content safety</span>: per-tab process isolation,
                same-origin policy, site isolation, the renderer
                sandbox, CSP, opaque-origin iframes.
              </p>
              <p class="aside">
                The crypto stack is the same story: WebCrypto
                AES-GCM, WebAuthn PRF, Subresource Integrity. peerd
                writes zero lines of cryptographic code.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="defense">
            <div class="glyph glyph--green" aria-hidden="true">2</div>
            <div>
              <h3>A spectrum of sandboxes.</h3>

              <p class="sub">// the primitive is free</p>
              <p>
                A sandbox is a sealed execution context built on a
                JavaScript isolate. Cloudflare leverages and markets V8
                isolates at datacenter scale and meters them by the
                invocation for AI sandboxes. peerd gets the same primitive
                for free: it's already in every tab and every worker the
                browser runs.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// one boundary per trust level</p>
              <p>
                peerd isn't stuck with one box. It picks the boundary by
                trust: the agent's own scripts run in a language-sealed
                Notebook; a compiled tool — a WASI binary: SQLite, a codec,
                a language runtime — runs inside that same sealed worker
                with zero ambient capability, seeing only the bytes it is
                handed; code built for you, or delivered peer-to-peer,
                runs in an opaque-origin iframe with a real origin
                boundary and not even any <code>chrome.*</code> access; a full
                POSIX program runs WASM-confined in a Linux VM. Untrusted
                code never runs in a weaker sandbox than it needs.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="defense">
            <div class="glyph glyph--green" aria-hidden="true">3</div>
            <div>
              <h3>The lethal trifecta, broken structurally.</h3>

              <p class="sub">// the failure mode</p>
              <p>
                Simon Willison's <em>lethal trifecta</em> (June 2025):
                an AI combining private data + untrusted content +
                an outbound network path is one prompt injection
                from exfiltrating anything it can reach. PromptArmor
                disclosed live exploits against Google Antigravity
                (late 2025) and Anthropic's Claude Cowork (January
                2026). Most browser-driving agents sit squarely in
                this failure mode.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// the structural fix</p>
              <p>
                peerd's main agent never reads raw page content. A
                disposable runner does: fresh context, no memory,
                no keys, no egress tools, no spawn, no code-eval.
                Even if injected, it has nothing to exfil through.
                Untrusted input and valuable capabilities are never
                in the same model context.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// defense in depth on top</p>
              <p>
                Every DOM read wraps its output as
                <code><untrusted_web_content></code>; the
                runner's summary is itself wrapped
                <code><untrusted_runner_summary></code> on the
                way back. An injection has to defeat two model
                contexts with two different framings to win.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="defense">
            <div class="glyph glyph--green" aria-hidden="true">4</div>
            <div>
              <h3>One egress chokepoint, top to bottom.</h3>

              <p class="sub">// two gates</p>
              <p>
                Provider traffic on a strict allowlist
                (<code>safeFetch</code>). Open-web HTTP(S) on a
                denylist (<code>webFetch</code>) blocking
                bank/health/identity/password-manager origins. Both
                audited on every call. WebVMs, Notebooks, and
                Apps all route through the same gates.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// what's structural, not policy</p>
              <p>
                The browser gives the VM no IP stack, so SSH, raw
                TCP/UDP, ICMP, SMTP, BitTorrent, and custom C2 protocols
                are not addressable. The extension's CSP pins plain
                HTTP to your configured local Ollama only;
                <code>http://</code> elsewhere is blocked at the
                manifest layer. HTTPS from inside the VM
                (<code>curl</code>, <code>wget</code>, <code>git</code>)
                is proxied through the same peerd-egress
                <code>webFetch</code> gate the agent itself uses,
                same denylist, same audit entry.
              </p>
              <p>
                And no third-party gateway. Provider traffic goes from
                your browser to the provider you configured. Application
                integrations, when they ship, go from your browser to the
                application's API. There is no peerd cloud service in the
                data path because there is no peerd cloud service.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// what isn't, honestly</p>
              <p>
                HTTPS to private-network IPs
                (<code>192.168.x</code>, <code>::1</code>,
                <code>*.local</code>) is still reachable, because the
                denylist matches host strings, not CIDR. A
                CIDR-aware private-IP gate is going into
                <code>webFetch</code> ahead of the denylist; code,
                not policy. Arbitrary-public-host C2 isn't solvable
                by any IP filter. That's bounded by the runner
                having no web tools at all.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="defense">
            <div class="glyph glyph--green" aria-hidden="true">5</div>
            <div>
              <h3>Credential isolation by construction.</h3>

              <p class="sub">// where the key lives</p>
              <p>
                Your model key never leaves the service worker. It's
                decrypted from the vault there and only there, used to
                build the <code>Authorization</code> header, and held
                in memory the whole time. The plaintext key never
                touches disk and is gone the moment the browser closes.
              </p>

              <p class="sub">// where it never goes</p>
              <p>
                No sandbox ever receives it. The Notebook, the App
                iframe, the Linux VM, the headless worker: none get
                the key, and none get an environment variable carrying
                it. They reach the network only by relaying through the
                same egress gate the agent uses. Untrusted code can't
                read a secret that was never placed where it runs.
                Isolation by architecture, not a credential proxy
                bolted in front.
              </p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>

        <div class="code-panel">
          <div class="head">
            <span>peerd-egress/fetch/safe-fetch.js</span>
            <span>↳ provider-allowlist gate</span>
          </div>
<pre><span class="tok-comment">// Hard egress allowlist for model-provider traffic. Even if the agent
// is fully prompt-injected and tries to POST your conversation to an
// attacker-controlled URL, this layer refuses. Fail closed.</span>
<span class="tok-keyword">const</span> HARDCODED_ALLOWLIST = Object.freeze([
  <span class="tok-string">'https://api.anthropic.com'</span>,
  <span class="tok-string">'https://api.openai.com'</span>,
  <span class="tok-string">'https://openrouter.ai'</span>,
  <span class="tok-string">'http://127.0.0.1:11434'</span>,   <span class="tok-comment">// local Ollama</span>
  <span class="tok-string">'http://localhost:11434'</span>,
]);

<span class="tok-keyword">export const</span> <span class="tok-fn">makeSafeFetch</span> = ({ getAllowlist, auditLog }) => <span class="tok-keyword">async</span> (resource, init) => {
  <span class="tok-keyword">const</span> origin = <span class="tok-fn">resolveOrigin</span>(resource);
  <span class="tok-keyword">if</span> (!<span class="tok-fn">getAllowlist</span>().<span class="tok-fn">includes</span>(origin)) {
    <span class="tok-keyword">await</span> <span class="tok-fn">auditLog</span>({ type: <span class="tok-string">'egress_denied'</span>, origin });
    <span class="tok-keyword">throw new</span> <span class="tok-error">EgressDeniedError</span>(origin);
  }
  <span class="tok-keyword">return</span> <span class="tok-fn">fetch</span>(resource, init);
};

<span class="tok-comment">// Open-web traffic (the agent's web tools + the VM's curl/wget) goes
// through peerd-egress/fetch/web-fetch.js. Same audit log, denylist
// gate instead of allowlist.</span></pre>
        </div>

        -->

      <!-- 05 — FAQ ================================================ -->
      <section id="faq" class="block-section faq-section" data-accent="amber">
        <div class="label">05, questions</div>
        <h2>FAQ</h2>

        <div class="faq-list">
          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Where does my data go?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              To the model provider you configured. That's it. peerd has
              no backend. Your conversations, vault contents, and API
              key never leave your machine except as outbound calls to
              the model you picked.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">BYOK and "no backend", but my prompts still go to the model, right?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Right, and we won't pretend otherwise. Your prompt (which can
              include page content) goes to the provider you chose:
              Anthropic, OpenRouter, or your own local Ollama, where nothing
              leaves the machine. There is no peerd server in the path, ever.
              "Client-side" means we can't see it; pick the provider whose
              terms you trust, or run local.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Do I need a paid API key?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Anthropic, OpenRouter, and Ollama (free, local) all ship
              today. Bring whichever key you want, or run local with no key
              and no bill. In-browser inference over WebGPU is next.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Can the agent see my bank, email, password manager?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Not by default. A sensitive-site denylist ships pre-loaded
              with hundreds of banks, health portals, password managers, and
              identity providers, editable in settings. Turn on Confirm
              before actions and nothing happens without your per-step
              approval.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Isn't a browser agent with broad permissions exactly the prompt-injection risk everyone's writing about?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Yes, it's the problem we built around first. The agent that
              holds your keys never reads a page; a throwaway runner with no
              keys and no network does, and its output comes back fenced as
              untrusted. Even a perfectly injected page has nothing to steal
              through. The cloud agents put untrusted content and your
              credentials in one model context; peerd never does.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">How is the Linux VM not a security hole?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              The VM is sandboxed by the tab, like everything else peerd
              runs in tabs, the same V8 isolate primitive Cloudflare uses
              for their AI agent code execution platform. Its network is
              HTTPS-only, gated by peerd's egress allowlist, the same
              gate the agent itself uses. The VM cannot open raw sockets,
              port-scan, SSH out, or pivot to your local network because
              browsers don't expose those capabilities to any code in any
              tab. The agent can do anything in the VM and your machine is
              not in the threat model. Structural, not policy.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">How is this different from Claude Code / OpenCode / Hermes?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Those live in your terminal. They can't see the page
              you're looking at, fill the form on your screen, or use
              the session you logged into. peerd lives in the
              browser; everything the browser sees, the agent sees.
              See <a href="#diff">section 01</a> for the full
              comparison matrix.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Is peerd really open source?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Yes, Apache 2.0. The extension code lives at
              <a href="https://github.com/NotASithLord/peerd" target="_blank" rel="noopener">github.com/NotASithLord/peerd</a>.
              CLA required for contributions; trademark held by Ariel
              Deschapell to prevent fork-confusion. The VM engine (CheerpX)
              is a commercial dependency today; we're migrating to
              v86 (BSD-2-Clause) down the road for a fully open stack.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Is peerd stable? What version is this?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              peerd is shipping as a v0.x developer preview today: install from
              source on GitHub. The architecture is stable; the surface is still
              being polished against real-world use. Chrome Web Store and Firefox
              AMO releases are coming soon. The version stays 0.x until the surface
              stabilizes.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">Why doesn't peerd support MCP?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              MCP exists to bridge agents to tools they can't otherwise
              reach. peerd doesn't need that bridge. Tabs replace MCP
              for application access, the agent reads the live
              DOM of any app you're logged into. <code>fetch</code>
              replaces MCP for APIs. WebVM replaces MCP for shell.
              WebRTC replaces MCP for agent-to-agent comms,
              <code>peerd-distributed</code> already runs a browser-to-browser
              network with private messaging and a DHT, with async (offline)
              messaging the next phase. Shipping MCP would dilute the thesis
              and add an exfiltration vector the rest of the security model
              exists to close.
            </p>
          </div>

          <div class="faq-row">
            <p class="faq-q">How is this different from Claude in Chrome, Nanobrowser, Comet?</p>
            <p class="faq-a">
              Those are mostly web-task automation tools focused on
              "go do this thing on a website." peerd is the broader
              developer agent harness, the browser-native
              equivalent of Claude Code or OpenCode, with real Linux
              VMs, voice, structural lethal-trifecta defense, and a
              peer-to-peer module (<code>peerd-distributed</code>)
              that ships its first wedge today and matures from there.
              Different scope, different audience, different
              architecture.
            </p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <p class="faq-more">
          More in the <a href="docs/#faq">docs FAQ</a>.
        </p>

    // ----- Wordmark crossfade on scroll ------------------------------
    // While the hero wordmark is visible, the nav wordmark is hidden.
    // Once the user has scrolled to the point where the hero wordmark is
    // about to be hidden by the sticky nav, we swap: hero fades+shrinks,
    // nav fades+settles in. Visually: the wordmark appears to "shrink
    // into" the nav slot.
    (function() {
      const heroWordmark = document.querySelector('.wordmark--hero');
      const navWordmark = document.querySelector('.wordmark--nav');
      const nav = document.querySelector('.nav');
      if (!heroWordmark || !navWordmark || !nav) return;

      let threshold = 0;
      function recompute() {
        // Compute the hero wordmark's bottom edge in document coordinates.
        // (BoundingClientRect is viewport-relative, so add scrollY to get doc coords.)
        const rect = heroWordmark.getBoundingClientRect();
        const wordmarkBottomDoc = rect.top + window.scrollY + rect.height;

        // The sticky nav covers the top of viewport. The hero wordmark
        // becomes hidden when its bottom edge passes below the nav's
        // bottom edge. Fire the swap a little earlier (40px) so the
        // animation feels in-step with the wordmark sliding behind nav,
        // not lagging afterwards.
        threshold = wordmarkBottomDoc - nav.offsetHeight - 40;
      }
      recompute();
      window.addEventListener('resize', recompute, { passive: true });
      // Also recompute after a tick in case fonts/layout finalize after first paint
      setTimeout(recompute, 200);

      let receded = false;
      let hasTypedOnce = false;
      function check() {
        const past = window.scrollY > threshold;
        if (past !== receded) {
          receded = past;
          heroWordmark.classList.toggle('is-receding', past);
          navWordmark.classList.toggle('is-emerging', past);

          // First time the nav wordmark emerges, play the typing animation.
          // Subsequent emergences fall through to the plain fade-in above.
          if (past && !hasTypedOnce) {
            hasTypedOnce = true;

            // Inject a cursor element for the typing animation.
            const cursor = document.createElement('span');
            cursor.className = 'wordmark-cursor--nav';
            cursor.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
            navWordmark.appendChild(cursor);

            // Trigger the typing CSS. Total animation runs ~600ms;
            // 700ms timeout gives a small buffer before cleanup.
            navWordmark.classList.add('is-typing');
            setTimeout(() => {
              navWordmark.classList.remove('is-typing');
              cursor.remove();
            }, 700);
          }
        }
      }
      window.addEventListener('scroll', check, { passive: true });
      check();
    })();

    // ----- Footer wordmark typing animation on scroll-to ---------------
    //
    // Independent of the nav wordmark logic. The footer wordmark sits
    // statically in the page (always visible by default via
    // .wordmark--footer), but the typing animation fires once the
    // first time it enters the viewport. After that it stays in its
    // colored end-state forever.
    (() => {
      const footerWordmark = document.querySelector('.wordmark--footer');
      if (!footerWordmark || typeof IntersectionObserver === 'undefined') return;

      let hasTyped = false;
      const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
        for (const entry of entries) {
          if (entry.isIntersecting && !hasTyped) {
            hasTyped = true;

            const cursor = document.createElement('span');
            cursor.className = 'wordmark-cursor--nav';
            cursor.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
            footerWordmark.appendChild(cursor);

            footerWordmark.classList.add('is-typing');
            setTimeout(() => {
              footerWordmark.classList.remove('is-typing');
              cursor.remove();
            }, 700);

            observer.disconnect();
          }
        }
      }, { threshold: 0.3 });

      observer.observe(footerWordmark);
    })();

    // ----- §02 h2 cycling noun typewriter ----------------------------
    //
    // The §02 heading reads "The browser is the [X]." where [X] cycles
    // through four words via a typewriter effect:
    //   runtime → network (italic) → hypervisor → operating system (italic).
    // The italic pair signals the more conceptual / architectural reading
    // of the claim; the upright pair the more literal one. Solves the
    // duplication of the original "The browser is the runtime. The browser
    // is the hypervisor." structure — now one claim, four cycling words.
    //
    // IntersectionObserver gates the cycle to when §02 is actually in
    // view, so we don't burn frames animating something the user can't
    // see. Once §02 leaves view the loop pauses; re-entering view
    // resumes from the current state.
    //
    // Reduced-motion users get "runtime" rendered statically with no
    // cursor — the cycle is decorative; the sr-only span carries the
    // full meaning for assistive tech.
    //
    // Timings are ~15% tighter than the original two-word cycle to keep
    // the loop tempo brisk now that there are four words to get through.
    (() => {
      const nounEl   = document.querySelector('.h2-cycle-noun');
      const textEl   = document.querySelector('.h2-cycle-text');
      const cursorEl = document.querySelector('.h2-cycle-cursor');
      if (!nounEl || !textEl) return;

      // Each entry: text to type, plus whether to italicize while typing.
      const words = [
        { text: 'runtime.',          italic: false },
        { text: 'network.',          italic: true  },
        { text: 'hypervisor.',       italic: false },
        { text: 'operating system.', italic: true  },
      ];

      const TYPE_DELAY  = 50;    // was 60 — ~15% faster
      const ERASE_DELAY = 30;    // was 35 — ~15% faster
      const READ_PAUSE  = 3000;  // was 3500 — ~15% faster
      const BLANK_PAUSE = 215;   // was 250 — ~15% faster

      const prefersReduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
      if (prefersReduced) {
        textEl.textContent = words[0].text;
        textEl.classList.toggle('italic', words[0].italic);
        cursorEl?.remove();
        return;
      }

      const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

      const typeInto = async (el, text, delay) => {
        for (let i = 0; i <= text.length; i++) {
          el.textContent = text.slice(0, i);
          await sleep(delay);
        }
      };

      const eraseFrom = async (el, delay) => {
        while (el.textContent.length > 0) {
          el.textContent = el.textContent.slice(0, -1);
          await sleep(delay);
        }
      };

      // Gate the cycle to when §02 is in view.
      let visible = false;
      let running = false;
      const section = document.getElementById('why-browser');

      if (section && typeof IntersectionObserver !== 'undefined') {
        const obs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
          for (const entry of entries) {
            visible = entry.isIntersecting;
            if (visible && !running) startCycle();
          }
        }, { threshold: 0.15 });
        obs.observe(section);
      } else {
        startCycle();
      }

      async function startCycle() {
        if (running) return;
        running = true;
        let idx = 0;
        // Brief initial pause so the cursor blinks visibly before typing starts.
        await sleep(600);
        while (visible) {
          const word = words[idx];
          // Toggle italic on the text element BEFORE typing — the whole
          // word renders italic or not, cursor stays upright (sibling).
          textEl.classList.toggle('italic', word.italic);
          await typeInto(textEl, word.text, TYPE_DELAY);
          await sleep(READ_PAUSE);
          if (!visible) break;
          await eraseFrom(textEl, ERASE_DELAY);
          await sleep(BLANK_PAUSE);
          idx = (idx + 1) % words.length;
        }
        running = false;
      }
    })();

    // ----- Install tabs ----------------------------------------------
    //
    // Tabbed installer (chrome / firefox / github). Click a tab — swap
    // aria-selected, .is-active on the tab, show the matching panel.
    (() => {
      const tabs = document.querySelectorAll('.install-tab');
      const panels = document.querySelectorAll('.install-panel');
      if (!tabs.length) return;

      tabs.forEach((tab) => {
        tab.addEventListener('click', () => {

          tabs.forEach((t) => {

    // ----- hero wordmark: high-res ANSI hover twin --------------------
    // Renders the wordmark to an offscreen canvas (real blocks, real
    // letters, real font), reads the pixels back, snaps each one to the
    // brand palette, and emits Unicode half-block glyphs — ▀ fg=top px /
    // bg=bottom px — for 2× vertical resolution per character cell (the
    // pretext / classic ANSI-art technique). The palette snap is what
    // keeps it on-brand: without it, canvas anti-aliasing produces
    // dozens of muddy in-between tints that read as fuzz at character
    // resolution. Built lazily on idle so first hover is instant and
    // initial page render pays nothing.
    (() => {
      const zone = document.getElementById('hero-wordmark-zone');
      const pre  = document.getElementById('wordmark-ansi');
      if (!zone || !pre) return;
      // hover is the only trigger — skip entirely on touch-primary devices
      if (window.matchMedia('(hover: none)').matches) return;

      const COLORS  = ['#00B7EB', '#EF4444', '#F59E0B', '#22C55E', '#D946EF'];
      const LETTERS = ['p', 'e', 'e', 'r', 'd'];
      const WHITE   = [250, 250, 250];
      const CELL = 24;                  // canvas px per block (square)
      const W = CELL * 5, H = CELL;     // 120 × 24 source-pixel grid

      const rgb = (h) => [parseInt(h.slice(1, 3), 16), parseInt(h.slice(3, 5), 16), parseInt(h.slice(5, 7), 16)];
      const BRAND = COLORS.map(rgb);

      let built = false;
      const build = async () => {
        if (built) return;
        built = true;

        // the canvas letters must use the loaded display font, or the
        // rasterised letterforms won't match the wordmark's
        try { await document.fonts.load('700 25px "Geist Mono"'); } catch {}

        const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
        canvas.width = W;
        canvas.height = H;
        const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });

        // five brand blocks, outer corners rounded like the CSS wordmark
        const r = Math.max(1, Math.round(CELL * 0.08));
        for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
          ctx.fillStyle = COLORS[i];
          ctx.beginPath();
          if (ctx.roundRect) {
            ctx.roundRect(i * CELL, 0, CELL, CELL,
              i === 0 ? [r, 0, 0, r] : i === 4 ? [0, r, r, 0] : 0);
          } else {
            ctx.rect(i * CELL, 0, CELL, CELL);
          }
          ctx.fill();
        }
        ctx.fillStyle = '#FAFAFA';
        ctx.font = '700 25px "Geist Mono", "JetBrains Mono", monospace';
        ctx.textAlign = 'center';
        ctx.textBaseline = 'middle';
        for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
          ctx.fillText(LETTERS[i], i * CELL + CELL / 2, CELL / 2 + 1);
        }

        // snap every pixel to: null (transparent) | white | its block colour.
        // The 1.6 bias means a pixel must be CLEARLY white to stay white —
        // anti-aliased letter edges fall back to the block colour instead of
        // speckling a white halo around each letterform.
        const img = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, W, H).data;
        const px = new Array(W * H);
        for (let y = 0; y < H; y++) {
          for (let x = 0; x < W; x++) {
            const o = (y * W + x) * 4;
            if (img[o + 3] < 128) { px[y * W + x] = null; continue; }
            const bi = Math.min(4, (x / CELL) | 0);
            const b = BRAND[bi];
            const dw = (img[o] - WHITE[0]) ** 2 + (img[o + 1] - WHITE[1]) ** 2 + (img[o + 2] - WHITE[2]) ** 2;
            const db = (img[o] - b[0]) ** 2 + (img[o + 1] - b[1]) ** 2 + (img[o + 2] - b[2]) ** 2;
            px[y * W + x] = dw * 1.6 < db ? '#FAFAFA' : COLORS[bi];
          }
        }

        // emit half-block rows, merging same-style runs into one span
        let html = '';
        for (let y = 0; y < H; y += 2) {
          let row = '', runFg = false, runBg = false, run = '';
          const flush = () => {
            if (!run) return;
            row += (runFg || runBg)
              ? `<span style="color:${runFg || 'transparent'};background-color:${runBg || 'transparent'}">${run}</span>`
              : `<span>${run}</span>`;
            run = '';
          };
          for (let x = 0; x < W; x++) {
            const top = px[y * W + x];
            const bot = px[(y + 1) * W + x];
            // cell → glyph + style: ▀ paints the top half in `color`, the
            // bottom half shows `background-color`; a bottom-only pixel
            // must use ▄ (bg would bleed into the empty top half otherwise)
            let ch, fg, bg;
            if (top && bot)       { ch = '▀'; fg = top;  bg = bot;  }
            else if (top)         { ch = '▀'; fg = top;  bg = null; }
            else if (bot)         { ch = '▄'; fg = bot;  bg = null; }
            else                  { ch = ' '; fg = null; bg = null; }
            if (fg !== runFg || bg !== runBg) { flush(); runFg = fg; runBg = bg; }
            run += ch;
          }
          flush();
          html += row + '\n';
        }
        pre.innerHTML = html;

        fit();
        pre.classList.add('is-ready');
      };

      // fit the natural text block to the CSS wordmark's exact box —
      // offsetWidth/Height ignore transforms, so a mid-recede measure
      // still reads the true footprint. Re-run on every hover: the idle
      // build can race the webfont load (stale glyph metrics) and the
      // responsive --size can change between visits to the hero.
      const fit = () => {
        const target = zone.querySelector('.wordmark--hero');
        const tw = target ? target.offsetWidth  : 300;
        const th = target ? target.offsetHeight : 60;
        pre.style.transform = 'none';
        const nw = pre.scrollWidth, nh = pre.scrollHeight;
        if (nw && nh) pre.style.transform = `scale(${tw / nw}, ${th / nh})`;
      };

      if ('requestIdleCallback' in window) requestIdleCallback(() => build(), { timeout: 4000 });
      else setTimeout(build, 2500);
      zone.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => { built ? fit() : build(); });
    })();

    // ----- §02 WebVM auto-boot on scroll-into-view -------------------
    // The terminal panel hosts an iframe to /vm-demo/, which is served
    // COOP+COEP isolated under the marketing site's headers so CheerpX
    // can flip crossOriginIsolated=true. We don't set src until the
    // panel actually enters the viewport — visitors who never reach §02
    // pay zero CheerpX bandwidth, and visitors who do see the boot
    // sequence themselves (which is part of the demo).
    (() => {
      const panel  = document.getElementById('vm-terminal-panel');
      const iframe = document.getElementById('vm-iframe');
      if (!panel || !iframe) return;

      const boot = () => {
        if (iframe.src) return;
        iframe.src = '/vm-demo/';
      };

      if (typeof IntersectionObserver === 'undefined') {
        // Conservative fallback: boot only if the panel is on-screen
        // at first render — otherwise wait for a scroll event.
        const rect = panel.getBoundingClientRect();
        const inView = rect.top < window.innerHeight && rect.bottom > 0;
        if (inView) boot();
        else window.addEventListener('scroll', boot, { once: true, passive: true });
        return;
      }

      // Fire when the panel actually enters view — no rootMargin
      // pre-roll, because watching the boot happen is part of the
      // show. threshold 0.1 = "panel is visibly entering" rather than
      // "one pixel of it just nicked the viewport".
      const obs = new IntersectionObserver(
        (entries) => {
          for (const e of entries) {
            if (e.isIntersecting) {
              boot();
              obs.disconnect();
              return;
            }
          }
        },
        { threshold: 0.1 },
      );
      obs.observe(panel);
    })();

    // ----- §02 collapsible primitive cards ---------------------------
    // The card header is a real <button>, so keyboard activation
    // (Space/Enter) works for free. We toggle aria-expanded on the
    // header and a .bp--open class on the card; the CSS animates the
    // grid-template-rows 0fr → 1fr and rotates the chevron.
    document.querySelectorAll('.bp-head').forEach((head) => {
      head.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const card = head.closest('.bp');
        if (!card) return;
        const open = !card.classList.contains('bp--open');
        card.classList.toggle('bp--open', open);
        head.setAttribute('aria-expanded', open ? 'true' : 'false');
      });
    });


    // ----- bfcache restore: replay the hero render -------------------
    // why: navigating back from docs (or any other page) restores the
    // home page from bfcache without re-executing CSS animations, so the
    // hero wordmark would sit fully drawn instead of typing in. Clone-
    // and-replace the hero wordmark to reset its animation state, then
    // jump to top so the user lands on the reveal.
    window.addEventListener('pageshow', (e) => {
      if (!e.persisted) return;
      const hero = document.querySelector('.wordmark--hero');
      if (!hero) return;
      const fresh = hero.cloneNode(true);
      fresh.classList.remove('is-receding');
      hero.replaceWith(fresh);
      window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'auto' });
    });
  </script>
